etymology: From the Old English sceabb and Old Norse skabb, a crust or roughness upon the skin; kin to the adjective shabby. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew sappachath and mispachath, the scaly eruption which the priest was commanded to examine under the law of the plague of leprosy.
biblical_def: A scab is a scaly eruption of the skin, and in Leviticus 13 it is the very thing the priest was appointed to look upon. The law did not tell the Israelite to judge his own flesh. “When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh like the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest” (Lev 13:2). He was brought. He did not diagnose himself, and he did not take a vote of his neighbours; he stood before the appointed examiner and waited on the verdict. The priest shut him up seven days and looked again, and if the plague spread not, “the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab” (Lev 13:6). But if it spread, the sentence was the other way: “it is a leprosy” (Lev 13:8). Two men might carry the same mark and receive opposite verdicts, and the difference was not in the man’s opinion of himself but in what the plague did over time under a lawful eye. Isaiah turns the word upon the proud: “the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion” (Isa 3:17), where the ornament was, there the sore shall be. So the scab in Scripture is the small beginning that must be examined, because a spot which spreads is no longer a spot.
webster_summary: An incrusted substance, dry and rough, formed over a sore in healing; a mangy or scaly eruption of the skin; the itch.
webster_full: SCAB, an incrustation or crust of dried matter formed over a wound or sore in the process of healing.
The itch or mange in animals; a scaly or crusted eruption upon the skin of man.
From Saxon sceabb; allied to Old Norse skabb, and to the Latin scabies, roughness, from scabo, to scratch.
In the Levitical law the scab is the symptom the priest examines and re-examines before he pronounces clean or unclean (Lev 13:2–8).
Figuratively, a small and superficial defilement which may prove to be a deep and spreading one.
scriptures: Lev 13:2

When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh like the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest, or unto one of his sons the priests:
Lev 13:6

And the priest shall look on him again the seventh day: and, behold, if the plague be somewhat dark, and the plague spread not in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean.
Lev 13:8
And if the priest see that, behold, the scab spreadeth in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a leprosy.
Isa 3:17
Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts.
corruption_summary: The scab was diagnosed by an appointed examiner, never by the man himself; the live corruption is a religion of self-assessment, where every man is his own priest over his own sin and always pronounces himself clean.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 13 is a standing rebuke to self-diagnosis. God did not leave the Israelite to decide whether the spot on his arm was nothing; He gave him a priest, a law, a waiting period, and a second look. Modern religion has reversed this entirely. The reigning assumption is that no one outside a man may name what is wrong inside him — that conscience is a private court with no appeal, that a sin is only a sin if the sinner agrees, and that any outside verdict is an intrusion. So the churches have quietly retired church discipline, elders no longer look on the plague, and the man with a spreading sore is congratulated on his honesty and sent home unexamined. Then the thing spreads, as Moses said it would, and what might have been dealt with as “but a scab” is at last a leprosy that costs a marriage, a ministry, or a soul.

Recover the appointed examiner. Scripture never flatters the sinner’s reading of himself: the heart is deceitful above all things, and he that trusteth in his own heart is a fool. God gave His church the ministry of the word and the office of elder precisely so that sin might be looked upon by a lawful eye and named for what it is. That is not cruelty; it is the mercy the leper never got until he was brought. And the priest of Leviticus was a shadow: the great High Priest looks on the plague of the heart, and He alone can pronounce clean not by finding no spot but by taking the uncleanness upon Himself. The man who submits to examination now has a Physician; the man who examines himself and acquits himself has only a spreading sore and a good opinion.
roots_summary: A crust upon the skin; in the law, the small symptom that must be brought to the priest and looked upon twice.
roots_lines: Scab — Saxon sceabb, Norse skabb, akin to Latin scabies, roughness.
Hebrew sappachath / mispachath, the scaly eruption of Leviticus 13.
The man does not judge it; he is brought unto the priest (Lev 13:2).
Seven days, then a second look — the verdict turns on whether it spreads (Lev 13:6–8).
Isaiah sets the scab where the ornament was, upon the crown of the proud (Isa 3:17).
usage: It is but a scab — the verdict of the priest, not the opinion of the patient.
A spot that spreads is no longer a spot; that is why the law required a second look.
Where the daughters of Zion wore their ornament, the LORD promised a scab (Isa 3:17).

etymology: From the Old English byl or byle, a swelling or sore, kin to the German Beule; unrelated in origin to the verb to boil, which comes through French from the Latin bullire. It renders the Hebrew shechin, an inflamed ulcer or burning sore.
biblical_def: The boil is an inflamed and burning ulcer of the flesh, and Scripture puts it in three places that must be held together. It is a plague upon Egypt: the ashes of the furnace became “a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast” (Exo 9:9), until the magicians who had matched Moses trick for trick “could not stand before Moses because of the boils” (Exo 9:11) — the sorcerers driven from the field by their own skin. It is the affliction of the righteous man: Satan “smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown” (Job 2:7), and Job scraped himself with a potsherd among the ashes. Mark what that verse establishes. The devil struck the blow, but he struck it only within the bounds the LORD had set, so that the boil of Job is at once a work of Satan and a providence of God, without contradiction and without excusing the tempter. And it is the sickness that God heals by means: Hezekiah lay dying, and “Isaiah said, Take a lump of figs. And they took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered” (2Ki 20:7). A word from the LORD had promised fifteen years; a poultice of figs was still applied. The promise did not make the figs superfluous, and the figs did not make the promise unnecessary.
webster_summary: A tumor or inflamed swelling upon the flesh which suppurates; an angry sore or ulcer breaking forth upon the skin.
webster_full: BOIL, a tumor upon the flesh, accompanied with inflammation and suppuration; an angry swelling or sore.
From Saxon byl, a swelling; the same word as the German Beule. Distinct from the verb to boil, Latin bullire.
The sixth plague of Egypt was a boil breaking forth with blains upon man and beast (Exo 9:9–11).
Job was smitten with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown (Job 2:7).
Hezekiah’s boil was healed after a lump of figs was laid upon it at the prophet’s word (2Ki 20:7; Isa 38:21).
scriptures: Exo 9:9
And it shall become small dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall be a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast, throughout all the land of Egypt.
Exo 9:11
And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; for the boil was upon the magicians, and upon all the Egyptians.
Job 2:7
So went Satan forth from the presence of the LORD, and smote Job with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown.
And Isaiah said, Take a lump of figs. And they took and laid it on the boil, and he recovered.
corruption_summary: The boil of Job and the boil of Hezekiah together destroy the health-and-wealth doctrine: the most upright man in the East was covered with sores, and the king whom God promised to heal was still given a poultice.
corruption_paragraphs: The Word-of-Faith and health-and-wealth teachers — Kenyon, Hagin, Copeland, and the prosperity preachers who followed them — hold that bodily healing is guaranteed in the atonement and may be claimed on demand, so that continuing sickness proves a defect of faith in the sufferer. Job settles the question in two verses. The LORD Himself calls Job perfect and upright, one that feared God and eschewed evil, and it is precisely that man who is covered with boils from sole to crown. His friends preached the prosperity doctrine at him for thirty chapters, reasoning backward from his sores to his supposed secret sin, and God ended the book by telling Eliphaz that His wrath was kindled against them, for they had not spoken of Him the thing that was right. The apostolic record says the same: Paul’s thorn was not removed but answered with sufficient grace (2Co 12:7–9), Timothy kept his often infirmities and was told to take a little wine (1Ti 5:23), and Trophimus was left at Miletum sick (2Ti 4:20). A doctrine that cannot account for Job, Paul, Timothy, and Trophimus is not a doctrine of Scripture, and it is cruel at the bedside besides.

The opposite error is fatalism, and Hezekiah’s boil forbids that too. God had already sworn to add fifteen years to the king’s life; the outcome was fixed by divine decree and could not fail. And still Isaiah said, take a lump of figs and lay it on the boil. The Reformed doctrine of providence has always insisted that God ordains the end and the means together, so that the certainty of the end is the very reason to use the means, not an excuse to despise them. He who decreed that Hezekiah should live decreed the figs. So the believer prays and takes the medicine, trusts the LORD and calls the physician, and does both without the least embarrassment. Presumption says God will heal, so refuse the means; fatalism says God has decided, so the means are pointless; Scripture says the God who appoints the recovery appoints the poultice, and the sufferer is to use what is set before him and leave the issue with Him.
roots_summary: A burning ulcer of the flesh — plague upon Egypt, trial of Job, and the sickness God healed by means.
roots_lines: Boil — Saxon byl, a swelling; German Beule; not from Latin bullire.
Hebrew shechin, an inflamed and burning sore.
Egypt’s sixth plague drove the magicians from the field (Exo 9:11).
Satan smote Job with boils, but only within the bounds God had set (Job 2:7).
Hezekiah’s recovery was promised by God and applied with figs (2Ki 20:7).
usage: From the sole of his foot unto his crown — the measure of Job’s affliction, and of his patience.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils; the sorcerer is not exempt from the plague.
Take a lump of figs: the promise of God and the use of means are not rivals.

etymology: From Middle English balled, bare or shining; the noun formed with the Saxon ending -ness, the state of wanting hair upon the head. It renders the Hebrew qorchah and qarachath, a bald place, especially one deliberately made by shaving in grief.
biblical_def: Baldness in Scripture is very seldom a matter of age and very often a matter of mourning. When Isaiah lists the judgments coming upon the finery of the daughters of Zion, the shaved head stands among them: “instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty” (Isa 3:24). Every ornament is exchanged for its opposite; the whole verse is a reversal, and baldness is what beauty comes to when God visits pride. Micah commands it upon the nation as a sign of exile: “Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee” (Mic 1:16). Amos sets it in the same rank: sackcloth upon all loins, baldness upon every head, the mourning of an only son (Amo 8:10). Yet the law drew a hard line around the practice. The priests were forbidden it outright: “They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh” (Lev 21:5), and Deuteronomy lays the same prohibition on all Israel as the sons of the LORD their God. The heathen gashed and shaved themselves for the dead. Israel might grieve, and grieve deeply, but she might not grieve like a people who worshipped death.
webster_summary: The want of hair upon the top of the head; in Scripture, the head shaved bare as a token of grief, disgrace, or divine judgment.
webster_full: BALDNESS, want of hair on the top of the head; the state of being bald.
By extension, meanness or inelegance of writing, wanting ornament; also, want of natural covering.
From bald, Middle English balled, bare, shining; whence the sense of nakedness on the crown.
In Scripture, a token of mourning and of judgment: “instead of well set hair baldness” (Isa 3:24).
The law forbade the priests, and Israel with them, to make baldness for the dead after the heathen manner (Lev 21:5; Deu 14:1).
scriptures: Isa 3:24

And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness; and instead of a stomacher a girding of sackcloth; and burning instead of beauty.
Mic 1:16
Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee.
Amo 8:10

And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only son, and the end thereof as a bitter day.
Lev 21:5
They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 3 is a judgment upon an age that made an idol of appearance; and the law against making baldness and cuttings for the dead still stands against grief that turns upon the body.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 3 reads like an inventory of a boutique — the tinkling ornaments, the cauls, the round tires like the moon, the chains, the bracelets, the mufflers, the changeable suits of apparel — and the LORD promises to answer the whole catalogue with stink, rent, baldness, sackcloth, and burning. The sin named is not clothing but the heart that lives for it: the daughters of Zion walked with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes. Our own age has industrialised that heart. An entire economy is built on persuading men and women that their worth is what the mirror reports, and it sells the remedy for baldness with the same breath that it sells the shame of it. Scripture does not forbid a woman to be lovely or a man to be well kept; it forbids the soul to rest there. Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, and the woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised — a verdict that outlives every hairline.

The second corruption is nearer to grief itself. The heathen neighbours of Israel shaved their heads bare and cut their flesh for the dead, and God forbade His people both, not because sorrow is wrong but because that sorrow was a false worship: it treated the body as the place to pay a debt to the dead and it mourned as those which have no hope. The same instinct has returned in our day whenever sorrow is turned inward upon the flesh with a blade. The answer then and now is not a stiffened lip but a better hope. Israel wept and rent her garments; Jesus wept at the grave of Lazarus; the men who buried Stephen made great lamentation over him. Christian grief is loud and honest and it is bounded, because the same Lord who was moved with compassion has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel.
roots_summary: A head made bare — in the prophets a sign of mourning, captivity, and beauty overthrown by judgment.
roots_lines: Baldness — from Middle English balled, bare or shining, with the Saxon -ness.
Hebrew qorchah, a bald place, most often one deliberately shaved in grief.
Isaiah sets it against “well set hair” in the great reversal of Zion’s finery (Isa 3:24).
Micah and Amos make it the badge of captivity and of a nation’s lamentation (Mic 1:16; Amo 8:10).
The law forbade baldness and cuttings made for the dead after the heathen manner (Lev 21:5).
usage: Instead of well set hair baldness — every ornament exchanged for its opposite.
Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle: mourn as one whose children are gone into captivity.
Israel might grieve deeply, but she might not grieve as the heathen grieved (Lev 21:5).

etymology: From the Latin febris, a fever, through the Old English fefor; the burning heat of the body in sickness. In the Greek of the Gospels it is puretos, from pur, fire — the body on fire.
biblical_def: A fever is the burning of the body in sickness, and the Greek word for it is built on the word for fire. It stands first among the covenant curses of Deuteronomy: “The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning” (Deu 28:22) — four words for heat piled one upon another against a nation that would not obey. Against that dark background the Gospels set a small and tender scene. “And when Jesus was come into Peter’s house, he saw his wife’s mother laid, and sick of a fever. And he touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them” (Mat 8:14–15). Luke, the physician, says that Christ stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her (Luk 4:39) — the same word he uses of the LORD rebuking devils and the wind. The fever obeys Him as the sea does. Two things deserve marking. First, He touched her; He did not send word from the doorway. Second, the healing was whole and immediate: no convalescence, no weakness, but she rose that same hour and served the household. Christ’s cures do not leave a man an invalid. The nobleman’s son at Capernaum was mended the same way, and the father learned the hour and believed (Joh 4:52). What the curse burned, the Son of God cooled with a touch.
webster_summary: A disease characterized by an accelerated pulse, heat, and thirst; the burning of the body in sickness.
webster_full: FEVER, a disease or morbid state of the system, characterized by increased heat, an accelerated pulse, thirst, and a diminution of strength.
From the Latin febris; Saxon fefor. The Greek puretos is from pur, fire.
Figuratively, any heat or agitation of the mind resembling the heat of the body in disease.
Fever stands among the covenant curses pronounced upon a disobedient Israel (Deu 28:22).
Christ rebuked the fever of Peter’s wife’s mother and it left her, and she arose and ministered (Luk 4:39; Mat 8:15).
scriptures: Mat 8:14
And when Jesus was come into Peter's house, he saw his wife's mother laid, and sick of a fever.
Mat 8:15
And he touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them.
Luk 4:39
And he stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them.

The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish.
corruption_summary: Christ rebuked a fever because He is Lord over it; the corruption is the modern healer who copies the gesture without the authority and then blames the sick man when the fever stays.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Luke says that Christ rebuked the fever, a whole industry of modern healers has taken up the verb. Sickness is addressed as though it were a demon to be scolded, congregations are taught to command their symptoms, and the failure of the fever to depart is laid at the door of the sufferer’s faith. This is a theft of an office. Christ rebuked the fever on the same authority by which He rebuked the wind and the unclean spirits — He is the Lord of the body He made, and the miracles of the Gospels were signs authenticating the Son of God, not a technique published for general use. When the apostles healed, they healed openly, completely, instantly, and never charged for it; they also left Trophimus sick at Miletum. Any ministry that promises what the apostles did not promise, and then explains its failures by accusing the afflicted, has departed from the record it claims to imitate.

The right use of these verses is warmer than the false one. Deuteronomy 28 tells us that fever entered the world by the curse; sickness is not an accident of matter but a mark of a world under sentence, and every burning night is a small notice that we are dust and under judgment. Then Matthew 8 tells us what the Son of God does with the curse: He walks into a fisherman’s house, sees a woman laid low, touches her hand, and the fire goes out. He did not have to touch her, and that is the point — the same hand would be nailed to a tree to bear the curse itself, and Matthew says a few verses later that He took our infirmities and bare our sicknesses. The believer under a fever prays for that hand, uses the means God provides, and rests either way; the fever leaves at His word now, or it leaves at the resurrection, and both are His doing.
roots_summary: The body on fire — a curse-word in Deuteronomy, a word Christ rebuked in Peter’s house.
roots_lines: Fever — Latin febris, Saxon fefor; the burning heat of sickness.
Greek puretos, from pur, fire — the Gospels call it a burning.
Deuteronomy ranks it among the covenant curses upon disobedience (Deu 28:22).
Christ touched the hand of Peter’s wife’s mother and the fever left her (Mat 8:15).
Luke says He rebuked it, the word used of devils and the wind (Luk 4:39).
usage: Sick of a fever — and He touched her hand, when a word would have served.
The fever left her, and she arose and ministered: Christ’s cures leave no convalescence.
He rebuked the fever as He rebuked the wind, because both are His creatures.

etymology: From the Latin consumptio, a using up or wasting away, from consumere, to devour utterly. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew shachepheth, a wasting disease, and kalah, a full end or determined destruction.
biblical_def: Consumption in the Authorized Version is the wasting away of a body or a nation until nothing is left. It appears first among the covenant curses. If Israel would not hearken, the LORD said, “I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart” (Lev 26:16); and Deuteronomy repeats it at the head of its list of plagues, “a consumption, and a fever, and an inflammation” (Deu 28:22). These are not general misfortunes attached loosely to disobedience. They are appointed, sworn, and covenantal — the sanctions of a treaty between the LORD and a people He had redeemed out of Egypt, and the wasting of the body is set forth as the visible shape of a wasting covenant life. The word then rises from the sickbed to the nation. Isaiah uses it of judgment upon Israel herself: “yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness” (Isa 10:22), where the very ruin is righteous and yet a remnant is spared through it. And he widens it to the whole earth: “I have heard from the Lord GOD of hosts a consumption, even determined upon the whole earth” (Isa 28:22). So the word carries both senses at once — the slow ebbing of flesh in a sick man, and the determined end which God has decreed for a world that will not repent.
webster_summary: A wasting of flesh and strength by disease; also, a using up or destruction; in the prophets, a decreed and determined ruin.
webster_full: CONSUMPTION, the act of consuming, or state of being consumed, wasted, or destroyed.
In medicine, a wasting of flesh and strength, with cough, hectic fever, and difficult breathing; a phthisis.
From the Latin consumptio, from consumere, to take up wholly, to devour.
Among the covenant curses of the law, appointed over a disobedient Israel (Lev 26:16; Deu 28:22).
In the prophets, a determined destruction decreed by the Lord GOD of hosts (Isa 10:22; Isa 28:22).
scriptures: I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart: and ye shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it.

The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish.
For though thy people Israel be as the sand of the sea, yet a remnant of them shall return: the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness.
Now therefore be ye not mockers, lest your bands be made strong: for I have heard from the Lord GOD of hosts a consumption, even determined upon the whole earth.
corruption_summary: The covenant curses are read as primitive superstition or reduced to natural consequence; Scripture presents them as appointed sanctions of a God who governs nations and keeps His word both ways.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 are among the chapters most quietly abandoned in the modern pulpit. Where they are handled at all, they are commonly explained away in one of two directions: either as the residue of an ancient people’s belief that sickness follows sin, now outgrown, or as mere natural consequence, so that God is left holding no appointment in the matter and disease simply happens. The text will not bear either handling. The LORD says I will appoint over you, the LORD shall smite thee — first person, active, sworn. A God who cannot send a fever cannot send a Saviour; the arm that is shortened for judgment is shortened for salvation too. And the same chapters that pronounce the curses pronounce the blessings in the identical voice, so that a people who will not have Him as Judge do not get to keep Him as Benefactor.

Two guards must be set on the doctrine, and Scripture sets them both. The first is Job: the covenant sanctions are addressed to a nation under a covenant, not converted into a rule by which any onlooker may read a particular man’s sickness backward to a particular sin. Christ set the same guard over the man born blind, and over the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices — think ye that they were sinners above all others? I tell you, Nay. The second guard is the remnant. Isaiah says the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness, and in the same breath that a remnant shall return; the wasting is real, the decree is fixed, and mercy runs through the middle of it. That is the pattern of the whole Bible: a consumption determined upon the whole earth, and a people preserved through the fire by the blood of the Lamb.
roots_summary: A wasting away — of flesh under disease, and of a nation under a decreed and righteous judgment.
roots_lines: Consumption — Latin consumptio, from consumere, to devour utterly.
Hebrew shachepheth, a wasting sickness; also kalah, a full and determined end.
Appointed by the LORD among the covenant curses of the law (Lev 26:16).
Deuteronomy sets it at the head of the plagues, with fever and inflammation (Deu 28:22).
Isaiah enlarges it to a consumption determined upon the whole earth (Isa 28:22).
usage: I will even appoint over you terror, consumption — the curse is sworn, not incidental.
The consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness: the ruin itself is just.
A remnant shall return — mercy runs through the middle of the decreed wasting.

etymology: From the Latin in-, not, and curabilis, that may be healed, from cura, care or cure. It renders the Hebrew anash, desperately sick, and its cognates — a wound past the reach of any remedy man can bring.
biblical_def: Incurable is the word Scripture uses when every remedy has been tried and the wound is still open. Jeremiah is its home. “For thus saith the LORD, Thy bruise is incurable, and thy wound is grievous” (Jer 30:12), and the next verse shuts every door: there is none to plead thy cause, thou hast no healing medicines. Then the diagnosis is pressed home to its cause — “thy sorrow is incurable for the multitude of thine iniquity: because thy sins were increased, I have done these things unto thee” (Jer 30:15). The wound is incurable because the sin is the disease and the LORD Himself struck the blow. The prophet knew it in his own body too: “Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed?” (Jer 15:18). Micah says the same of Samaria’s wound, and the Chronicler records that the LORD smote Jehoram in his bowels with an incurable disease. Then comes the turn that makes this word gospel. Five verses after pronouncing the case hopeless, the same LORD says: “For I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds” (Jer 30:17). Nothing in the patient has changed. The wound is exactly as incurable as it was. What has changed is that the Physician who wounded has resolved to heal, and He does it because they called her an Outcast, whom no man seeketh after.
webster_summary: That cannot be healed or remedied; past the reach of medicine; in Scripture, a wound no man can bind and only God can heal.
webster_full: INCURABLE, that cannot be cured; not admitting of remedy; irremediable.
Hence, not admitting of correction or reformation; hopeless in a moral sense.
From the Latin in, not, and curabilis, curable, from cura, care, cure.
Jeremiah uses it of Zion’s bruise, and traces the incurableness to the multitude of her iniquity (Jer 30:12, 15).
The same chapter answers it: “I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds” (Jer 30:17).
scriptures: For thus saith the LORD, Thy bruise is incurable, and thy wound is grievous.
Why criest thou for thine affliction? thy sorrow is incurable for the multitude of thine iniquity: because thy sins were increased, I have done these things unto thee.
For I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds, saith the LORD; because they called thee an Outcast, saying, This is Zion, whom no man seeketh after.
Why is my pain perpetual, and my wound incurable, which refuseth to be healed? wilt thou be altogether unto me as a liar, and as waters that fail?
corruption_summary: Flattened into a purely medical word, incurable loses the doctrine it was made to carry: the sinner’s case is hopeless in itself, and that is precisely the ground of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: In ordinary modern speech incurable belongs to the clinic and nowhere else; it is a prognosis, and its whole freight is despair. Scripture uses it in a larger register, and something essential is lost when the larger register goes. Jeremiah 30 is a diagnosis of the soul as much as of the city: the bruise is incurable, there is none to plead the cause, there are no healing medicines. That is total depravity stated in the language of the sickbed — not that man is as bad as he could be, but that his case is past self-help, past reformation, past every remedy the patient or his friends can bring. The modern gospel that offers Christ as an improvement to a manageable condition has not read the chart. Until a man knows his wound is incurable, he will keep trying poultices; and the whole doctrine of grace waits on that discovery.

The second loss is the answer. Because the word has been surrendered to the clinic, believers hear incurable and think only of the end; Jeremiah says it and then says I will restore health unto thee. Mark the logic, for it is the logic of the gospel entire. God does not heal because the wound proved treatable after all. He heals against the diagnosis, sovereignly, on a ground located wholly in Himself — because they called thee an Outcast, whom no man seeketh after. The very fact that no man sought her is given as the reason the LORD did. So the sinner is not asked to find some curable remainder in himself to present as a basis of hope. He is asked to confess the wound incurable and to look away to the One who was Himself wounded, by whose stripes we are healed. Ezekiel’s heart of stone is not repaired; it is taken out and replaced. That is what God does with the incurable.
roots_summary: Past all remedy — the exact word Jeremiah uses for Zion’s wound, and the exact ground on which God heals it.
roots_lines: Incurable — Latin in-, not, plus curabilis, from cura, cure.
Hebrew anash, desperately sick, past binding up.
Jeremiah: the bruise is incurable and there are no healing medicines (Jer 30:12–13).
The cause is named — the multitude of thine iniquity (Jer 30:15).
The cure is sovereign — I will restore health unto thee (Jer 30:17).
usage: Thy bruise is incurable: the diagnosis that must precede any real cure.
Incurable for the multitude of thine iniquity — sin is the disease, not the symptom.
He heals against the diagnosis, and the reason is in Himself alone (Jer 30:17).

etymology: From the Latin medicina, the healing art or a remedy, from medeor, to heal. It renders the Hebrew gehah, a cure, and teruphah, a healing or remedy — that which is applied to a wound to make it whole.
biblical_def: Medicine in Scripture is a remedy applied to a wound, and the Bible speaks of it without the least suspicion. Proverbs makes the boldest use of the word: “A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones” (Pro 17:22). The state of the soul works upon the body as a remedy works upon a sore; gladness in God is medicinal, and settled sorrow wastes the frame. Ezekiel sets medicine at the end of his temple vision, where the river runs out from the sanctuary and the trees upon its banks bear fruit for meat and their leaf for medicine (Eze 47:12) — a picture the Revelation takes up when the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations. So the ultimate medicine flows from the sanctuary, from God Himself. But the word also stands in the prophets as a warning. Jeremiah says of Egypt, “in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured” (Jer 46:11), and of Zion, “thou hast no healing medicines” (Jer 30:13). Medicines are real, lawful, and often effectual, and they are not almighty. There is a wound they cannot reach, and a nation that piles up remedies while refusing the LORD is heaping up figs against a mortal disease. Balm grows in Gilead; the question Jeremiah asks is why the health of the daughter of his people is not recovered.
webster_summary: Any substance administered for the cure of disease; the healing art; whatever serves to remedy or restore.
webster_full: MEDICINE, any substance, simple or compound, administered to a sick person for the cure or alleviation of disease.
The art of preventing, curing, or alleviating the diseases of the human body.
Figuratively, anything which serves to cure or correct a moral malady.
From the Latin medicina, from medeor, to heal, to cure.
Scripture uses it of a merry heart (Pro 17:22) and of the leaf of the tree by the sanctuary river (Eze 47:12).
scriptures: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.

And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine.
There is none to plead thy cause, that thou mayest be bound up: thou hast no healing medicines.
Go up into Gilead, and take balm, O virgin, the daughter of Egypt: in vain shalt thou use many medicines; for thou shalt not be cured.
corruption_summary: Two errors flank the doctrine of means: the sect that calls medicine unbelief, and the age that makes medicine its god; Scripture blesses the remedy and refuses it the throne.
corruption_paragraphs: On one side stand those who despise the means. Christian Science denies the reality of the disease outright; the harder wing of the Word-of-Faith movement treats a prescription as a confession of doubt, and children have died in that doctrine. Scripture gives it no quarter. Isaiah ordered a poultice of figs for a king whose recovery God had already sworn (2Ki 20:7). Paul told Timothy to leave off water and take a little wine for his stomach’s sake and his often infirmities (1Ti 5:23). Luke, the beloved physician, is named as such by the Holy Ghost without a word of apology (Col 4:14). And Christ Himself said that they that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick (Luk 5:31) — an argument that assumes the physician’s office is good and useful, or the illustration collapses. To use the means God provides is not to distrust Him; it is to receive what He has given.

On the other side stands our own age, which has done to medicine what Judah did to Egypt: leaned on it as a saviour. Jeremiah’s taunt is exact — in vain shalt thou use many medicines, for thou shalt not be cured. When a civilisation can transplant an organ but cannot tell a man why he was made, it has multiplied remedies and lost the cure. Asa is the standing warning: in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians, and the Chronicler records it as a fault, not for consulting them but for seeking to them instead of God. The Reformed doctrine of means walks between both ditches. God ordinarily works through second causes, so the believer takes the medicine, keeps the appointment, and thanks God for the physician; and God is never bound by the means, so the believer prays, submits, and knows that the leaf which finally heals the nations grows by a river that issues out of the sanctuary.
roots_summary: A remedy applied to a wound — lawful, often effectual, never almighty.
roots_lines: Medicine — Latin medicina, from medeor, to heal.
Hebrew gehah, a cure; teruphah, a remedy or healing.
A merry heart works upon the body as a medicine works upon a sore (Pro 17:22).
The healing leaf grows by a river issuing out of the sanctuary (Eze 47:12).
Many medicines cannot cure a wound God has struck (Jer 46:11; Jer 30:13).
usage: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine — gladness in God is medicinal.
Thou hast no healing medicines: the case that only God can take.
Take the medicine and pray; the God who appoints the cure appoints the means.

etymology: From the Latin cura, care, and curare, to take care of, to heal; through the Old French curer. Hence a cure is both the care taken and the healing effected — whence also the old sense of a minister’s cure of souls.
biblical_def: To cure is to heal a disease through — to make an end of it, not merely to ease it. The Authorized Version keeps the word for cases where a real and finished restoration is in view. Christ “gave power and authority over all devils, and to cure diseases” to the twelve (Luk 9:1), and when the disciples failed with the lunatick child, the father’s complaint was exactly this: “I brought him to thy disciples, and they could not cure him” (Mat 17:16). The Master could and did. But the great use of the word is national and spiritual. Hosea watches Ephraim discover his sickness and run to Assyria for the remedy: “yet could he not heal you, nor cure you of your wound” (Hos 5:13). The wound was inflicted by God, and no political alliance could touch it. Then Jeremiah, writing over a city already doomed, gives the promise: “Behold, I will bring it health and cure, and I will cure them, and will reveal unto them the abundance of peace and truth” (Jer 33:6). Note that the cure and the revelation come together — health of the nation and the abundance of peace and truth, body and doctrine in one gift. Scripture never offers a cure that leaves the truth unrevealed. The old English usage held both senses honestly: a man had the cure of souls before he ever had a cure for a fever.
webster_summary: A healing; the removal of disease or complaint, and restoration to health; also, care, oversight, or spiritual charge.
webster_full: CURE, a healing; the act of healing; restoration to health from disease, or to soundness after a wound.
A remedy for disease; that which heals or removes an evil.
Care, charge, or oversight; as, the cure of souls committed to a minister.
From the Latin cura, care, and curare, to take care of, to heal; Old French curer.
Christ gave the twelve authority to cure diseases (Luk 9:1); the LORD promises to bring Jerusalem health and cure (Jer 33:6).
scriptures: Jer 33:6
Behold, I will bring it health and cure, and I will cure them, and will reveal unto them the abundance of peace and truth.
Hos 5:13
When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah saw his wound, then went Ephraim to the Assyrian, and sent to king Jareb: yet could he not heal you, nor cure you of your wound.
And I brought him to thy disciples, and they could not cure him.
Luk 9:1
Then he called his twelve disciples together, and gave them power and authority over all devils, and to cure diseases.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a clinical or therapeutic word, cure loses its older and larger sense; the cure of souls is exchanged for the management of feelings, and the sinner is treated where he should be saved.
corruption_paragraphs: For most of English history a minister held a cure of souls, and the phrase meant what it said: a charge of men and women whose deepest disease he was set to treat by the word of God. That vocabulary has almost vanished, and with it the office it named. In its place a great deal of the modern church has adopted the therapeutic register wholesale — the pulpit offers coping and self-care, sin is renamed as brokenness or an unhealthy pattern, guilt is treated as a feeling to be managed rather than a verdict to be answered, and the word healing is used almost exclusively of the emotions. The exchange looks compassionate and is not. Hosea shows why: Ephraim saw his sickness and went to Assyria, which is to say he took a real wound to a remedy that could not reach it, and the prophet’s comment is flat — he could not cure you of your wound. Every remedy that does not deal with God deals with the symptom.

Recover the older sense, and the two halves of Jeremiah 33:6 hold together. God promises health and cure, and in the same breath the revelation of the abundance of peace and truth. He does not offer relief without doctrine, nor doctrine without relief. This is not a contempt for ordinary care of the body or of the mind; the Lord who made the frame gave us physicians, and a Christian may take counsel and take medicine and give thanks for both. It is a refusal to let the lesser cure stand in the place of the greater. A man may be steadied in his nerves and still be under wrath; the cure Scripture presses is the one that reconciles him to God through the blood of the cross, and every other mercy hangs beneath it. Christ said He came for the sick, and He named the disease before He offered the cure.
roots_summary: Care and healing in one word — from the Latin cura, whence both the cure of a fever and the cure of souls.
roots_lines: Cure — Latin cura, care; curare, to take care of, to heal.
The old English sense is a charge of souls before it is a remedy for bodies.
Christ gave the twelve authority to cure diseases (Luk 9:1).
Ephraim carried a God-given wound to Assyria and was not cured (Hos 5:13).
God promises health and cure together with peace and truth revealed (Jer 33:6).
usage: They could not cure him — the disciples’ failure, and the Master’s ease.
He could not cure you of your wound: no ally heals what God has struck.
Health and cure, with the abundance of peace and truth — never one without the other.

etymology: The older English spelling of plaster, from the Latin emplastrum and Greek emplastron, a salve spread upon a surface, from emplassein, to daub on. The Authorized Version keeps the one word for both a medicinal poultice laid on a sore and the mortar daubed upon a wall.
biblical_def: A plaister is anything spread on — a salve laid upon the flesh, or mortar laid upon a wall — and the Authorized Version uses the single word for both. In its medical sense it appears at one of the great sickbeds of the Old Testament. Hezekiah had turned his face to the wall and wept; God added fifteen years to his life and gave him the sign of the shadow going backward; and then, quietly, “Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover” (Isa 38:21). The promise was already sure. The plaister was applied anyway. In its building sense it belongs to the law of the leprous house: when the infected stones were taken out and cast into an unclean place, the owner took other stones and other morter and “shall plaister the house” (Lev 14:42), and if the plague broke out again after it was plaistered, the house was pulled down. Fresh plaister could cover a wall; it could not cure a plague that had gone into the fabric. Moses commanded another plaister at the Jordan: great stones set up and plaistered, and all the words of the law written plainly upon them (Deu 27:2). And on a plaistered palace wall at Babylon a hand wrote MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN while the king’s knees smote together (Dan 5:5). Law and doom alike were written on plaister.
webster_summary: A salve or medicinal application spread upon cloth and laid on the body; also mortar or a composition spread upon walls.
webster_full: PLAISTER, the older orthography of plaster; a substance spread upon a surface, whether flesh or wall.
In pharmacy, an external application of a consistency harder than ointment, spread on cloth and applied to the body.
In building, a composition of lime, water, and sand, used for coating walls and partitions.
From the Latin emplastrum, Greek emplastron, from emplassein, to daub or spread on.
The Authorized Version uses it of the figs laid on Hezekiah’s boil (Isa 38:21) and of the mortar of the leprous house (Lev 14:42).
scriptures: For Isaiah had said, Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover.
And they shall take other stones, and put them in the place of those stones; and he shall take other morter, and shall plaister the house.
Deu 27:2
And it shall be on the day when ye shall pass over Jordan unto the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee, that thou shalt set thee up great stones, and plaister them with plaister:
Dan 5:5
In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote.
corruption_summary: An archaic spelling for a poultice or mortar; the abiding lesson is that a plaister may be a lawful means of healing or a mere covering over a plague, and the difference is everything.
corruption_paragraphs: The live danger with this word is not a redefinition but a confusion of its two uses. Isaiah’s figs were a genuine means: God had promised the king fifteen years, and the prophet still ordered the poultice, so that the certainty of the decree and the diligence of the remedy stood together in one sickroom. Leviticus 14 shows the other case. A house with the plague in its stones could be scraped, re-stoned, and plaistered afresh; but if the plague came again, no amount of new mortar would save it, and the house came down. Ezekiel names the sin exactly — the prophets who daubed the wall with untempered morter, promising peace where there was no peace, so that the smooth coat hid a wall already leaning. Every generation is tempted to plaister what God says must be pulled down: a marriage patched with resolutions and no repentance, a church tidied with programmes while its foundation shifts, a conscience smoothed with religious duty while the plague lives in the stones.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain doctrine of means. God ordains ends and appoints the second causes that reach them, so that a believing man may take up a lump of figs without the least suspicion that he is distrusting the promise, and may lean wholly on the promise without despising the figs. Deuteronomy 27 adds the other half: the plaistered stones at the Jordan carried the words of the law written very plainly, and Belshazzar’s plaistered wall carried his sentence. Plaister is a surface, and what is written on it, or hidden under it, is the whole question. Let the believer use every lawful remedy for the body, and let him refuse every remedy that only covers the soul.
roots_summary: Anything spread on — the figs on Hezekiah’s boil, the morter on the leprous house, the wall that bore Belshazzar’s doom.
roots_lines: Plaister — older spelling of plaster; Latin emplastrum, Greek emplastron.
From emplassein, to daub or spread upon a surface.
A poultice of figs was laid on Hezekiah’s boil though God had already promised his life (Isa 38:21).
The leprous house was re-stoned and plaistered, and pulled down if the plague returned (Lev 14:42–45).
Law was written on plaistered stones at Jordan; judgment on a plaistered wall at Babylon (Deu 27:2; Dan 5:5).
usage: Lay it for a plaister upon the boil — the means used under a promise already sure.
Fresh plaister may cover a wall; it cannot cure a plague in the stones.
On plaister the law was written plainly, and on plaister the king read his sentence.

etymology: A plain English compound of dung and hill — the heap of refuse and manure outside a house or city. It renders the Hebrew ashpoth, a rubbish heap, and the Aramaic nevalu, a ruin or dunghill; the lowest and filthiest place a man could be found.
biblical_def: The dunghill is the refuse heap outside the gate, where the sweepings of a city and the dung of its beasts were cast, and where the destitute lay because there was nowhere lower to go. Scripture uses it almost always to measure a distance. Hannah sings it first: “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory” (1Sa 2:8). The Psalmist takes up her line and repeats it as settled doctrine about the character of God: “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill” (Psa 113:7), and the next verse says why — that he may set him with princes. Jeremiah measures a fall by the same heap: they that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets, and they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills (Lam 4:5). Daniel records the Chaldean threat to make a man’s house a dunghill, and Christ Himself ends His parable of savourless salt there — it is neither fit for the land, nor yet for the dunghill; but men cast it out (Luk 14:35). Below the dunghill there is nothing. That is exactly why the LORD is said to reach into it: the beggar is not lifted from a promising position but from the refuse, and the throne of glory is at the other end of that lift.
webster_summary: A heap of dung and refuse cast outside a dwelling or city; hence any mean, vile, or lowest situation.
webster_full: DUNGHILL, a heap of dung; a place where dung and the refuse of a house or city are laid.
Any mean or vile abode or condition; a place of filth and contempt.
As an adjective, sprung from the dunghill; mean; low; base.
A plain compound of dung and hill, rendering the Hebrew ashpoth, a rubbish heap.
Hannah and the Psalmist both make it the place from which God lifts the beggar to sit among princes (1Sa 2:8; Psa 113:7).
scriptures: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S, and he hath set the world upon them.
He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill;
Lam 4:5
They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills.
It is neither fit for the land, nor yet for the dunghill; but men cast it out. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.
corruption_summary: Hannah’s song is regularly read as a manifesto of social reversal; it is a confession of sovereign grace — the LORD Himself lifts a particular beggar from a particular dunghill because it pleases Him to do it.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation theology and its evangelical imitators have made 1 Samuel 2 and the Magnificat that echoes it into a political programme: the poor as a class are the subject, reversal is the plot, and the church’s business is to bring the reversal about. The text will not sit still for it. Hannah is not describing a movement; she is describing a Person, and every verb belongs to Him — the LORD killeth and maketh alive, He bringeth low and lifteth up, He raiseth the poor, He lifteth the beggar, He setteth them among princes. The reason given in the same verse is not economic but metaphysical: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD’S, and He hath set the world upon them. He may lift whom He will because He owns the ground. Strip that out and Hannah’s song becomes a slogan; leave it in and it is the doctrine of sovereign, particular, undeserved grace sung by a woman who had been barren and was now a mother.

Recover the personal edge of the verse, for that is where its comfort lies. The dunghill is where a man is found by grace, not where he is left. Scripture is candid about what we bring to the transaction — our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and Paul counted his best religious credentials as dung that he might win Christ. That is the same heap. The gospel does not say that God saw promise in the beggar; it says the LORD lifted him from the refuse and set him among princes and gave him to inherit the throne of glory, and Job is the picture of it, sitting down among the ashes and raised up at the last. The doctrine humbles a man before it exalts him, and it keeps him humble after, because a prince who remembers the dunghill has nothing to boast of but the hand that reached in.
roots_summary: The refuse heap outside the gate — the lowest place a man can lie, and the place from which God lifts beggars to sit with princes.
roots_lines: Dunghill — a plain compound of dung and hill, the refuse heap of a house or city.
Hebrew ashpoth, a rubbish heap; Aramaic nevalu, a ruin.
Hannah sings that the LORD lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill (1Sa 2:8).
The Psalmist repeats it as settled doctrine of God’s character (Psa 113:7).
Savourless salt is fit neither for the land nor for the dunghill (Luk 14:35).
usage: He lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill — the verb belongs wholly to the LORD.
They that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills: the measure of a fall.
A prince who remembers the dunghill has nothing left to boast of.
